summary:
Imad Touil, Distinguished Engineer at QuantumBlack, frames his talk around the fact that AI-native organizations run on skills, and opens with an audience exercise showing that while many attendees have built skills, fewer share them within teams, and only a handful govern them across the organization.

He introduces an agentic software stack with two loops. The inner loop is the code/agent harness, containing a context manager, tools/MCPs, memory/state, and a skills loader. The outer loop holds workflows built from skills, sub-agents, MCP servers, and hooks. Supporting layers include sandbox environments, MCP gateway, model gateway, knowledge graph (covering IT, codebase, skills registry), workflow marketplace, and a context layer assembling project instructions, tool schemas, conversation memory, and retrieved content.

He notes the familiar specify/plan/task/implement loop is only one product-increment step within a far larger lifecycle spanning product strategy, market and customer research, discovery, data preparation, delivery, platform/ops, launch, and ongoing optimization. Real organizations run many such lifecycles in parallel.

Within a workflow, hooks only fire on events, sub-agents primarily protect the context window, and most organizations consume rather than build MCP servers, so actual know-how lives in skills. Without structured skills, workflows are not deterministic. Skills adoption accelerated from Anthropic's first skills article about eight months prior, to an open standard two months later, with most major agents pulling skills by February. SkillsBench showed clearly more deterministic outcomes with skills applied than without.

Touil proposes designing skills like microservices: reusable, modular, discoverable, portable across harnesses, specialized, composable, consistent, and cost-efficient via progressive disclosure. He composes regulation, retention policy, disclosure standards, GDPR, and template skills into a regulatory disclosure review workflow emitting auditable reports.

He warns ungoverned skills create a new technical debt: cross-team duplication, quality decay because skills must be retested against new models not just original tasks, no discoverability, no ownership, accidental non-composability, security risk since public skills carry executable scripts, and missing access control. The fix is a centralized platform with a searchable catalog and metadata, an MCP to query and a CLI to pull skills into IDE or sandbox, dependency tracking, versioning so harnesses auto-pull the latest, and access control. Governance is where technology stops solving it, requiring named human owners across architecture, infrastructure, and security.

A six-month simulation across 15 teams of 5-12 engineers shows governed skills reduce duplication, improve quality and security ratios, and cut token cost by removing repeated prompting. The same approach must be applied to whole workflows, hosted on a centralized platform so the next engineer pulls, runs, tests, and improves them. He closes by urging skills registries, skills evaluation against Anthropic best practices, and caution around auto-evolving skills since closed-loop evolution without governance amplifies risk.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Three questions, and the hands that drop
sections.summary: Imad Touil introduces himself as a Distinguished Engineer at QuantumBlack and previews the talk's theme, that AI-native organizations run on skills. He polls the room: most have built and used skills, fewer share them within their teams, and only a handful govern them across the organization, motivating the rest of the talk.

sections.title: The agentic stack, inner loop and outer
sections.summary: He outlines an agentic software stack with an inner loop (context manager, tools/MCPs, memory/state, skills loader) and an outer loop of workflows (skills, sub-agents, MCP servers, hooks). Supporting enablement includes sandbox environments, MCP gateway, model gateway, knowledge graph over IT, codebase and skills registry, a workflow marketplace, and a context layer that assembles project instructions, tool schemas, conversation memory, and retrieved content.

sections.title: Why specify, plan, task, implement is one step
sections.summary: Touil argues the familiar specify/plan/task/implement sequence is only a single product-increment step. The real end-to-end lifecycle adds product strategy, market and customer research, discovery, data preparation, data product delivery, then loops back into the increment, and continues into platform/ops, launch, and ongoing optimization.

sections.title: What the full lifecycle actually contains
sections.summary: He walks through the lifecycle: defining product strategy and success metrics, conducting market research, competitive analysis and customer interviews, running discovery, preparing data and integrations, building data pipelines, validating data quality, and cataloging assets. He emphasizes that organizations run many parallel lifecycles across mobile, internal platforms, and customer-facing products.

sections.title: Organizations run many lifecycles, not one
sections.summary: Touil reinforces that one workflow cannot build everything an organization needs. Different delivery lifecycles coexist for mobile, departmental, internal employee, and customer-facing platforms, and after launch each enters a continuous loop of performance optimization, incident response, and re-planning.

sections.title: Where the know-how actually lives
sections.summary: He reviews workflow components: hooks fire on events, sub-agents exist mainly to minimize context window pressure, and most teams consume MCP servers rather than build them, so the actual organizational know-how lives in skills. Without structured skills, workflows are not deterministic. He traces rapid skills adoption from Anthropic's first article eight months prior to an open standard two months later, with broad agent adoption by February, and cites SkillsBench showing clearly more deterministic outcomes with skills than without.

sections.title: Designing skills like microservices
sections.summary: Touil proposes treating skills like microservices, applying reuse, modularity, discoverability, portability across harnesses via the shared standard, specialization, composability, consistency, and cost efficiency via progressive disclosure that loads the right skills at the right time to reduce token usage. He sketches a data retention policy skill as an example.

sections.title: Progressive disclosure and token cost
sections.summary: He elaborates that progressive disclosure delivers the right skills in the right amount at the right time, defining a new unit that makes organizational know-how executable, portable, and cheap while reducing token consumption.

sections.title: Composing regulation skills into an audit trail
sections.summary: He shows how a catalog of composable skills at the regulation level, including retention policy, disclosure standards, GDPR rules, and fill-in templates, can be pulled automatically by a regulatory disclosure review workflow at runtime to produce deterministic audit reports, identify improvements, and feed improvements back into the codebase.

sections.title: Ungoverned skills as technical debt
sections.summary: Touil warns that without governance, skills become a new class of technical debt. The first symptom is widespread duplication across teams that quietly converge on the same technology stack, leaving everyone to rebuild the same skill repeatedly.

sections.title: More symptoms of ungoverned skills: quality decay, ownership, composability, security, access control
sections.summary: He extends the technical-debt argument: skills must be validated against new models not only their original task or quality decays; without governance they are undiscoverable; ownership is unclear so no one maintains them; composability does not happen by default and needs a domain-driven approach; public skills carry executable scripts so pulling them without a security pipeline is a supply-chain risk; and not every skill should be accessible to everyone, so access control is crucial.

sections.title: What a central skills platform needs
sections.summary: Touil lays out the rollout: enable individuals to create, test, improve, and use skills through an agreed tool, then share and collaborate within teams on the same stack. Move to a centralized platform with a searchable catalog and metadata, an MCP to query the catalog and a CLI to pull skills into IDE or sandbox, dependency tracking, versioning and lifecycle so harnesses auto-pull the latest release, access control, and evaluation and observability.

sections.title: Governance, and who owns which domain
sections.summary: He is blunt that governance is where technology stops solving it. Architects, engineering leads, infra leads, and cyber leads must own their domains, ensure skills are updated per policy, and drive the change. When done right, every team pulls from one centralized place, executes high-quality skills, and pushes improvements back.

sections.title: Simulating fifteen teams over six months
sections.summary: He presents a simulation of 15 teams of 5-12 engineers over six months, tracking skills per engineer, average daily utilization, duplication ratio, and quality/security ratio. Without governance, mature teams differ wildly in productivity and cost; with governance, common ground emerges because the harness identifies an already-published skill and pulls it, solving duplication and quality/security issues.

sections.title: Applying the same idea to whole workflows
sections.summary: Touil argues skills are only one component of workflows; the same governance must apply to whole workflows. A centralized platform hosting workflows means the next engineer can tap into a workflow, build it with required skills, run and test it, and push improvements back for the organization to reuse.

sections.title: Registries, evaluation and auto evolving skills
sections.summary: He closes with three frontiers to explore: skills registries, already being centralized by IDP vendors; skills evaluation, where testing against Anthropic best practices is a simple heuristic for invocation and structure; and auto-evolving skills via closed loops, which he frames as the next hype and warns will amplify impact and risk without governance guardrails in place.

demonstrations: Composition of a regulation-level catalog (retention policy, disclosure standards, GDPR rules, fill-in templates) into a regulatory disclosure review workflow that emits deterministic audit reports and feeds improvements back into the codebase.

Six-month simulation across 15 teams of 5-12 engineers comparing ungoverned vs governed skills across productivity, average daily utilization, duplication ratio, quality, security, and token cost, showing governed skills reduce duplication and stabilize quality/security while cutting token spend.

Workflow-level reuse example where an engineer taps into a centralized workflow platform to provision infrastructure, build it with required skills, run and test it, then push improvements back to the centralized platform for the rest of the organization.
limitations: The simulation is illustrative and was created by the speaker rather than drawn from a real organization.
Auto-evolving skills via closed loops are described as a current hype without a proven governance playbook, and the speaker warns they amplify risk if used without guardrails.
Skills evaluation methodology is still an open discussion; the speaker's preferred heuristic is testing against Anthropic best practices.
Governance outcomes depend on how the organization is already structured, since architecture, infrastructure, and security leads must own domains.
quantitativeClaims: Eight months between Anthropic's first skills article and the talk.
Two months from that article to emergence of an open standard adopted by agent harnesses.
Most major agents had adopted the skills standard by February of the talk year.
SkillsBench showed clearly more deterministic outcomes when skills were applied versus running the same task without them against auto engineering and cybersecurity.
The full product lifecycle diagram shown represents roughly 10-20% of the real complexity, which varies by organization.
Simulation uses 15 teams of 5-12 engineers each, run across six months.
Internal Developer Portal (IDP) vendors are already centralizing skills registry capabilities, suggesting broad availability within months even if not present today.

organization.name: QuantumBlack
organization.summary: QuantumBlack is McKinsey & Company's AI consulting arm, branded QuantumBlack, AI by McKinsey. First-party McKinsey pages say it was born in Formula 1 analytics and now blends AI systems with McKinsey domain expertise as hybrid intelligence. QuantumBlack Labs is the in-house engineering and product group that publishes open-source agent tooling such as ARK. Imad Touil, a distinguished engineer at QuantumBlack, presents how AI-native organizations should structure and govern agent skills. Anthropic Agent Skills and SkillsBench are mentioned vendors and benchmarks, not the featured organization.
organization.status: McKinsey AI division as of the research date. Capability homepage, hybrid-intelligence approach page, Labs product page, official Medium engineering posts, and the McKinsey ARK repository are live. No ownership change since the August 2026 talk.
